header.title: System Card
header.subtitle: A plain-language record of how an AI product works and how it’s checked.

stories.label: 01 · Agent Stories
stories.title: Each Agent Has One Job and Clear Limits
stories.intro: Every role is written like a user story: what it’s for, what it can do, what it must never do, and how we know it worked.
stories.definition: An agent story is a user story adapted for an AI agent.

agents.name: Planner
agents.story: As the person orchestrating the build, when I think out loud in voice notes, I want them turned into specs and labeled instructions, so that each agent gets one clear task.
may: Write one labeled instruction per agent
never: Send instructions while I’m still giving notes
Present a guess as a fact
stops: The instruction is written and labeled for one agent
works: The builder needs no follow-up questions
The checklist that comes back matches what I asked for

agents.name: Builder
agents.story: As the person orchestrating the build, when I hand over a spec or a batch of notes, I want working code and course content, tested and live, so that I can judge the result instead of supervising the work.
may: Read the spec and the project rules
never: Make anything public or delete data without me
Swap in content before the judge’s review
Push without pulling and testing first
decides: Which checked sentences fit a lesson
stops: The batch is live with a Live / Not Done checklist, or a stop rule is reached

agents.name: Judge
agents.story: As the person orchestrating the build, when a builder finishes a course part or a screen, I want an independent review, so that the builder isn’t grading its own work.
may: Read every new sentence and screen
Mark each one Use, Reject, Keep, Fix or Cut
Score screens against the craft rubric
decides: Whether a sentence is natural, correct and right for A1
stops: The review file is written, with counts for each verdict
works: Every part is reviewed before it’s swapped in
Each fix names the line, the correction and the reason
The audits stay clean after the fixes

agents.name: Debugger
agents.story: As the person orchestrating the build, when something breaks on a real device, I want one fresh session on that one bug, so that the fix comes with a cause and a test.
may: Reproduce the bug on a simulated iPhone and iPad
never: Fix more than its one bug
decides: What only a real phone can confirm
stops: The fix is live with its test, or it reports that the cause wasn’t found and what it needs from the phone
works: The new test fails without the fix

outro: One builder splits its work among helper agents, each in its own copy of the code. A separate judge reviews the results. Each agent plans its own steps inside written rules.
The rules live in one file that every session reads first, so every change to them is tracked.

product.label: 02 · Product Definition
product.title: Who This Helps, Who It Doesn’t
product.intro: This section defines the product: who it helps, who it hands to teachers and real exams, and where it stops.

columns.title: Where it helps
items: Adults starting any of nine European languages from zero
Getting from reading to first conversations
Learners who stalled on gamified apps
Practicing for an official A1 exam
Reaching A1 with an honest measure of progress
Self-directed study with no locks or streaks
Ten-minute daily lessons
Travel tasks: ordering, directions, forms

columns.title: Where it might help
items: A2 learners reviewing the basics
Classroom learners who want extra practice
Heritage speakers filling gaps in reading and writing
Listening at natural speed
Pronunciation (record and compare, never graded)
Spain’s Spanish (the course teaches Latin American Spanish)
Portugal’s Portuguese (the course teaches Brazilian Portuguese)

columns.title: Where it hands off
items: Anything needing a native speaker’s ear (the content is AI-reviewed, not yet native-checked)
B1 and above
Certified proof of level (the official exams)
Children under 13
Graded pronunciation and accent coaching
Languages in other alphabets (Arabic, Greek, Asian languages)
Live conversation with a person (tutors, language exchanges)
Professional language (legal, medical, business)

scope.label: 03 · Model Scope
scope.title: How We Guide the Model, How the Model Guides the Learner
scope.intro: The lessons are fixed, checked content. The model steps in only where a live answer helps: conversation, explanations and notes on writing.
scope.goal: Help learners practice real conversation at their level.
scope.tableTitle: In and Out of Model’s Scope

rows.do: Definitions and verb forms from Wiktionary
Two or three, after the conversation
Repeat, slow down, spell, explain, in the language
One word and the right answer

outro: The pattern across every row: the model sets up the practice and reports honestly.
It never does the learning for the learner, and it never invents the facts.

spec.label: 04 · Behavioral Spec
spec.title: Behavioral Spec Inventory
spec.intro: Everything that tells the agents and the product how to behave.
spec.note: Counted from the repo, not estimated. CLAUDE.md is read first by every session, so a rule changed there reaches the next agent without anyone being told.

evaluation.label: 05 · Evaluation
evaluation.title: What the Agents Get Right, How We Know
evaluation.intro: Each row takes one industry term and points to the piece of this project that does that job, with a link to the tool or artifact.

rows.artifact: Every lesson of every course, built and walked: 250,125 questions across nine courses
Nine craft criteria scored 1 to 5, from “no dead time” to “obvious in one second”
An independent model session reviews every sentence batch and screen. It changes no code, and a person has the final word
A verdict on every sentence (Use, Reject, Keep, Fix, Cut), each with a reason

Every new word is shown before it’s tested, across 24,435 lessons in nine courses. The exception is 152 words that look the same in English, like taxi and train. No lesson adds more than four new words.
Every fixed bug gets a test that fails without the fix. 51 test files
A script taps through a real lesson on a simulated iPhone and iPad before every push
A fast check before each push (about 30 seconds for an engine-only change, 6.5 minutes for a French content change), the full suite on GitHub after
Coverage of each course’s A1 word list (an official list where one exists, a frequency list where none does): from 79% to 97% across the nine courses

Conversations and explanations run on Haiku 5.5; practice generation runs on Opus 5.5. Each conversation stops at 14 learner turns, each device gets 5 conversations and 30 explanations a day (kept in the browser), and a monthly spend limit on the Tamago workspace is the backstop
A limit per signed-in learner, enforced on the server. Today the server has none; the device caps above can be cleared
Learner flags (“my answer should be accepted”) collected for review
Native speakers checking the drafted sentences
